To the others he said in my hearing, Go through the city after him, and strike: don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity; kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is […]
echoes.note: The seal on the foreheads (9:4) reworks Ezekiel's mark (taw) set on the foreheads of those who sigh over abominations, so the destroyers pass them over; Ezek 9:6 'do not touch anyone on whom is the mark.' Same protective forehead-marking logic, shared with Rev 7:3. Strong typological and verbal correspondence (LXX sphragis / Rev sphragida; metopa, foreheads).

echoes.text: How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.
echoes.note: The 'star fallen from heaven to earth' (9:1) evokes Helel ben Shachar, the Day Star/Lucifer 'fallen from heaven' (14:12) cast down to Sheol/the Pit (14:15, LXX hadou). The fall + descent to the abyss/Pit and the personal agency ('to him... the key') support a figural reading of a fallen angelic being. Note Hebrew 'Helel' (Day Star) vs LXX 'heosphoros'; John echoes the trajectory more than the lexeme.

echoes.text: Who long for death, but it doesn’t come; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,
echoes.note: 9:6 'they will desire to die, and death will flee from them' closely matches Job 3:21, those 'who long for death, but it does not come; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures.' Shared paradox of death sought yet withheld; high verbal/thematic correspondence (LXX himeirontai tou thanatou).

echoes.text: He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and looked, and saw that the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace.
echoes.note: Smoke rising from the pit 'like the smoke from a burning furnace' (9:2) echoes Abraham seeing Sodom's destruction, 'the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace' (LXX hosei atmis kaminou). Shared furnace-smoke simile of cataclysmic judgment; the abyss takes on Sodom-like overtones.

echoes.text: Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: Sinai theophany: the mountain's 'smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace' (LXX hos kapnos kaminou). The same furnace-smoke phrase as Rev 9:2; a Sinai/judgment-theophany overtone alongside the Genesis 19 link. Identifying the exact source is difficult since the simile is stock OT idiom.

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: In Joel the locust-Day-of-the-LORD darkens sun and moon (2:10; cf. 2:2 'a day of darkness and gloom'); Rev 9:2 darkens 'the sun and the air' by the pit-smoke (per 9:2-3 sequence). Same eschatological darkening tied to the locust visitation, strengthening the Joel matrix already controlling the pericope.

echoes.text: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
echoes.note: The king's Hebrew name 'Abaddon' (9:11) is the OT term for the realm of destruction/Sheol, paired with Sheol in Job 26:6 ('Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering'). John personifies the place-name into the angel of the abyss; explicit Hebrew lexical borrowing (Abaddon).

echoes.text: Destruction and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.’
echoes.note: 'Abaddon and Death say...' (28:22) personifies Abaddon alongside Death, anticipating John's personalization of Abaddon as the angel-king of the abyss (9:11). Reinforces the Hebrew-Bible background of the name Apollyon glosses ('Destroyer'). LXX renders Abaddon as apoleia, the lexical bridge to Apollyon.

echoes.text: Sheol and Abaddon are before Yahweh— how much more then the hearts of the children of men!
echoes.note: 'Sheol and Abaddon are before the LORD' — another Abaddon/Sheol pairing in the wisdom corpus reinforcing the name's currency as a designation of the destructive underworld behind Rev 9:11.

echoes.text: For Yahweh will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood on the lintel, and on the two door posts, Yahweh will pass over the door, and will not allow the destroyer to come in to your houses to strike you.
echoes.note: The personified 'Destroyer' (ha-mashchit; LXX ho olothreuon) who passes through Egypt at Passover lies behind the title Apollyon ('Destroyer') in 9:11 — and behind the sparing of the forehead-sealed (9:4), since the Destroyer passes over the marked. Typological link between the destroying angel and the abyss-king.

echoes.text: Thus the Lord Yahweh showed me: and behold, he formed locusts in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and behold, it was the latter growth after the king’s harvest.
echoes.note: Amos's locust-swarm vision of judgment ('he formed locusts') is part of the prophetic locust-as-judgment tradition John draws on; faint and generic, contested as an independent source given the dominance of Joel and Exodus.

echoes.text: Your guards are like the locusts, and your officials like the swarms of locusts, which settle on the walls on a cold day, but when the sun appears, they flee away, and their place is not known where they are.
echoes.note: Nahum likens Nineveh's officials to swarming locusts that settle then flee; part of the locust-army-of-judgment topos. Faint, generic background to the locust-as-invading-host imagery of 9:7-10.

echoes.text: Yahweh of Armies has sworn by himself, saying, Surely I will fill you with men, as with the canker worm; and they shall lift up a shout against you.
echoes.note: 'I will fill you with men like locusts' — equating an invading army with locusts, the same conceptual fusion John performs (locusts shaped like cavalry). Faint, supports the army=locust metaphor rather than supplying specific diction.

echoes.text: The Midianites and the Amalekites and all the children of the east lay along in the valley like locusts for multitude; and their camels were without number, as the sand which is on the seashore for multitude.
echoes.note: Midian and the eastern peoples lay 'thick as locusts' for multitude — the locust-host-as-innumerable-army simile resonant with 9:3-10. Generic background image; low confidence as a discrete source.

pericopes.text: The sixth angel sounded. I heard a voice from the horns of the golden altar which is before God, saying to the sixth angel who had one trumpet, “Free the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates!” The four angels were freed who had been prepared for that hour and day and month and year, so that they might kill one third of mankind. The number of the armies of the horsemen was two hundred million. I heard the number of them. Thus I saw the horses in the vision, and those who sat on them, having breastplates of fiery red, hyacinth blue, and sulfur yellow; and the heads of lions. Out of their mouths proceed fire, smoke, and sulfur. By these three plagues were one third of mankind killed: by the fire, the smoke, and the sulfur, which proceeded out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths, and in their tails. For their tails are like serpents, and have heads, and with them they harm.

echoes.text: In that day Yahweh made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
echoes.note: 'The great river Euphrates' (9:14) is a fixed biblical phrase marking the ideal eastern boundary of the promised land (Gen 15:18 'to the great river, the river Euphrates'; LXX tou potamou tou megalou Euphratou). John's identical formula loads the Euphrates with covenant-boundary and threat-from-the-east significance (the direction of Israel's historic invaders).

echoes.text: Yahweh will utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his scorching wind he will wave his hand over the River, and will split it into seven streams, and cause men to march over in sandals.
echoes.note: Isaiah's eschatological drying/striking of 'the River' (Euphrates) to open a way echoes the Euphrates as the threshold the eastern hordes cross; the bound-then-freed angels at the river (9:14-15) work the same geography of judgment unleashed across the Euphrates. Cf. Rev 16:12 explicitly drying the Euphrates for kings from the east.

echoes.text: “You shall make an altar to burn incense on. You shall make it of acacia wood. Its length shall be a cubit, and its breadth a cubit. It shall be square, and its height shall be two cubits. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top, its sides around it, and its horns; and you shall make a gold molding around it.
echoes.note: 'The horns of the golden altar which is before God' (9:13) draws on the golden altar of incense with its four horns set before the LORD (Exod 30:1-3; cf. 30:10 atonement on its horns). The voice issuing from the altar's horns ties the trumpet judgment to the prayers/incense of the saints (Rev 8:3-5). Verbal and cultic correspondence.

echoes.text: The priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of sweet incense before Yahweh, which is in the Tent of Meeting; and he shall pour out all of rest of the blood of the bull at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
echoes.note: Blood placed on 'the horns of the altar of sweet incense before the LORD' — the sacrificial-horns idiom underlying 'the horns of the golden altar' in 9:13, reinforcing the Exodus 30 incense-altar background of the avenging voice.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.
echoes.note: The lethal triad fire/smoke/sulfur from the horses' mouths (9:17-18) reworks the LORD raining 'sulfur and fire' on Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24, LXX theion kai pyr), with the smoke of 19:28 completing the triad. The Sodom destruction pattern is the archetypal model for sulfurous divine judgment in Revelation (cf. 14:10; 19:20; 21:8).

echoes.text: On the wicked he will rain blazing coals; fire, sulfur, and scorching wind shall be the portion of their cup.
echoes.note: 'On the wicked he will rain coals, fire, and sulfur' (Ps 11:6 [LXX 10:6]) supplies the fire-and-sulfur judgment formula behind the three plagues of 9:17-18; reinforces the Sodom-pattern of brimstone judgment. LXX pyr kai theion parallels Rev's pyr... theion.

echoes.text: For a nation has come up on my land, strong, and without number. His teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he has the fangs of a lioness.
echoes.note: The cavalry's lion-headed mouths ('horses' heads resembled lions' heads,' 9:17) reprise the lion-toothed locust nation of Joel 1:6 (already echoed in 9:8), binding the sixth-trumpet army to the fifth-trumpet locusts and to Joel's invading host. Lion-mouth imagery of devouring judgment.

echoes.text: After this I saw in the night visions, and, behold, a fourth animal, awesome and powerful, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet: and it was diverse from all the animals that were before it; and it had ten horns.
echoes.note: The composite, monstrous, devouring war-beast with iron teeth that 'devoured and broke in pieces' resonates with the hybrid serpent-tailed, lion-mouthed cavalry of 9:17-19 as an instrument of mass slaughter. Faint; Daniel's beast tradition is broadly present in Revelation but not specifically cued here.

echoes.text: The snorting of his horses is heard from Dan: at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones the whole land trembles; for they have come, and have devoured the land and all that is in it; the city and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: The invading horses from Dan whose snorting 'is heard' and who 'devour the land' — the apocalyptic enemy cavalry trampling the people. A prophetic war-horse-of-judgment topos resonant with the 200-million horsemen of 9:16-17. Faint and generic.

echoes.text: Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves. Their horsemen press proudly on. Yes, their horsemen come from afar. They fly as an eagle that hurries to devour.
echoes.note: The Chaldean horses 'swifter than leopards... they fly like an eagle swooping to devour' — the terror-cavalry-of-judgment imagery behind the swarming horsemen of 9:16-17. Faint background to the invading-cavalry motif.

echoes.text: The chariots of God are tens of thousands and thousands of thousands. The Lord is among them, from Sinai, into the sanctuary.
echoes.note: 'The chariots of God are myriads, thousands upon thousands' supplies the innumerable-heavenly-host idiom behind the hyperbolic 'two hundred million' (dismyriades myriadon) horsemen of 9:16. Faint numerical-host parallel.

echoes.text: A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: 'Ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him' — the same myriads-of-myriads formula John uses to count the cavalry (9:16). Possible source of the numerical hyperbole, though applied here to an army of destruction rather than the heavenly court.

pericopes.text: The rest of mankind, who were not killed with these plagues, didn’t repent of the works of their hands, that they wouldn’t worship demons, and the idols of gold, and of silver, and of brass, and of stone, and of wood; which can neither see, nor hear, nor walk. They didn’t repent of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their sexual immorality, nor of their thefts.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat.
echoes.note: The catalogue of idols 'of silver and gold, the work of human hands' that cannot see, hear, or walk (Ps 115:4-7) is the template for 9:20 — 'the works of their hands... idols of gold, and of silver, and of brass, and of stone, and of wood... which can neither see, nor hear, nor walk' (so 9:20 per the WEB fuller form; cf. parallel). Strong verbal correspondence on the materials-list and 'works of their hands.'

echoes.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths.
echoes.note: Near-doublet of Ps 115: idols of silver and gold, work of human hands, with mouths/eyes/ears that do not function. Together with Ps 115 it forms the polemic-against-dead-idols matrix behind 9:20, reinforced by recurrence across the Psalter. LXX wording (erga cheiron anthropon) matches Rev's 'works of their hands.'

echoes.text: but have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before you, and you and your lords, your wives and your concubines, have drunk wine from them; and you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which don’t see, nor hear, nor know; and the God in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways, you have not glorified.
echoes.note: Belshazzar's indictment for praising 'the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know' (5:23) supplies the fullest five/six-material idol list closest to Rev 9:20's gold/silver/brass/stone/wood. Strong correspondence including the materials enumeration and the failure-to-honor-God-while-worshiping-idols frame.

echoes.text: There you shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.
echoes.note: 'Gods, the work of human hands, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell' — covenant-curse idol polemic feeding the 9:20 list (wood and stone, works of hands). Reinforces the standard Deuteronomic dead-idol formula behind John's catalogue.

echoes.text: I will utter my judgments against them touching all their wickedness, in that they have forsaken me, and have burned incense to other gods, and worshiped the works of their own hands.
echoes.note: Judgment 'because they have forsaken me and burned incense to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands' — the 'works of their hands' idiom for idolatry that John applies in 9:20 ('the works of their hands, that they wouldn't worship demons'). Idolatry-as-handiwork link.

echoes.text: They sacrificed to demons, not God, to gods that they didn’t know, to new gods that came up recently, which your fathers didn’t dread.
echoes.note: 'They sacrificed to demons, not to God' (LXX edaimoniois) is the OT root for John's striking gloss that idol-worship is demon-worship (9:20, 'worship demons, and the idols'). Ps 106:37 ('sacrificed their sons to demons') is the parallel. Establishes the demons-behind-idols theology rare in the OT.

echoes.text: Yes, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.
echoes.note: 'They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons' (LXX tois daimoniois) — together with Deut 32:17 the scriptural basis for equating idolatry with demon-worship in 9:20. Reinforces, with murders in the vice-list of 9:21, the demonic-bloodshed nexus.

echoes.text: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's extended satire on the craftsman who fashions a god from wood and metal that cannot save — the classic 'work of human hands' idol-mockery underlying 9:20's catalogue of materials. Thematic rather than verbatim; supports the dead-idol polemic.

echoes.text: You also carried the tent of your king and the shrine of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves.
echoes.note: Carrying idol-images one has made — prophetic idolatry indictment in the broad stream feeding 9:20; faint and generic compared to the Psalm/Daniel catalogues.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal.
echoes.note: The vice-list of 9:21 — murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, thefts — tracks the Decalogue's second-table prohibitions (you shall not murder / commit adultery / steal), with sorcery added (cf. Exod 22:18). John frames impenitence as persistence in covenant-breaking sins. Echo of the Decalogue's ethical core rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: “You shall not allow a sorceress to live.
echoes.note: 'You shall not allow a sorceress to live' anchors 'sorceries' (pharmakon) in the 9:21 vice-list within the Torah's condemnation of magic; cf. Deut 18:10-11. Supplements the Decalogue echo with the specifically prohibited sin of pharmakeia.

echoes.text: O Yahweh, don’t your eyes look on truth? You have stricken them, but they were not grieved. You have consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction. They have made their faces harder than a rock. They have refused to return.
echoes.note: 'You have struck them, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction... they refused to repent' — the prophetic motif of judgment failing to produce repentance, the precise dynamic of 9:20-21 ('did not repent'). Thematic background to the impenitence frame.

echoes.text: “I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in every town; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says Yahweh. “I also have withheld the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest; and I caused it to rain on one city, and caused it not to rain on another city. One place was rained on, and the piece where it didn’t rain withered. So two or three cities staggered to one city to drink water, and were not […]
echoes.note: The fivefold refrain 'yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD' after escalating plagues (famine, drought, blight, pestilence, overthrow like Sodom) is the structural model for 9:20-21: plagues that fail to bring repentance. Strong thematic/structural coherence with the trumpet sequence's purpose.

pericopes.text: I saw a mighty angel coming down out of the sky, clothed with a cloud. A rainbow was on his head. His face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire. He had in his hand a little open book. He set his right foot on the sea, and his left on the land. He cried with a loud voice, as a lion roars. When he cried, the seven thunders uttered their voices.

echoes.text: Above the expanse that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone; and on the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a man on it above. I saw as it were glowing metal, as the appearance of fire within it all around, from the appearance of his waist and upward; and from the appearance of his waist and downward I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him. As […]
echoes.note: The rainbow encircling the divine glory (Ezek 1:28, the bow in the cloud) supplies the angel's rainbow-crowned head and luminous appearance; strong on availability/recurrence (Ezekiel pervades Rev) and thematic coherence (theophanic glory). LXX iris matches Rev's iris.

echoes.text: I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz: his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
echoes.note: The radiant heavenly figure with face like lightning/sun, legs/feet like burnished bronze or fire, and a great voice. Verbal volume is high (face, feet/legs of fire, loud voice cluster together), strongly shaping the angel's theophanic description.

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night: the pillar of cloud by day, and the pillar of fire by night, didn’t depart from before the people.
echoes.note: The pillar of cloud and pillar of fire of the Exodus theophany underlie the conjunction 'clothed with a cloud' and 'feet like pillars of fire' (stuloi pyros). New-Exodus typology coheres with Revelation's plague structure; thematic coherence strong, verbal echo on 'pillar of fire.'

echoes.text: The lion has roared. Who will not fear? The Lord Yahweh has spoken. Who can but prophesy?
echoes.note: 'The lion has roared; who will not fear?' supplies the prophetic lion-roar simile and its link to inescapable prophetic speech (cf. v.7 prophets). Coheres with the immediately following 'as a lion roars.'

echoes.text: They will walk after Yahweh, who will roar like a lion; for he will roar, and the children will come trembling from the west.
echoes.note: 'He will roar like a lion... his children shall come trembling' associates the divine/messianic roar with the gathering of peoples, anticipating v.11's many peoples. Faint but recurrent lion-roar motif.

echoes.text: Yahweh will roar from Zion, and thunder from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth will shake; but Yahweh will be a refuge to his people, and a stronghold to the children of Israel.
echoes.note: 'The LORD roars from Zion' (Joel 4:16 MT) couples the divine roar with cosmic upheaval and judgment, fitting the thunder that follows. Thematic coherence with the seven thunders.

echoes.text: I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth. When I bring a cloud over the earth, that the rainbow will be seen in the cloud, and I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all flesh. The rainbow will be in the cloud. I will look at it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every […]
echoes.note: The bow in the cloud as covenant sign of mercy restrains judgment; the rainbow on the angel's head before the oath frames the interlude as grace amid the trumpet plagues. Reinforces the Ezek 1 rainbow.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled.
echoes.note: Sinai thunders (qolot, LXX phonai) accompanying theophany undergird the seven thunders 'uttering their voices.' Faint; the thunder-as-voice idiom is widespread.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s voice is on the waters. The God of glory thunders, even Yahweh on many waters. Yahweh’s voice is powerful. Yahweh’s voice is full of majesty. The voice of Yahweh breaks the cedars. Yes, Yahweh breaks in pieces the cedars of Lebanon. He makes them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young, wild ox. Yahweh’s voice strikes with flashes of lightning. Yahweh’s voice shakes the wilderness. Yahweh shakes the wilderness of Kadesh. […]
echoes.note: The sevenfold 'voice of the LORD' (qol YHWH) thundering over the waters is a plausible source for the SEVEN thunders specifically; Hebrew structures seven thunderings, a feature less visible in LXX. Contested but suggestive of the number.

pericopes.text: When the seven thunders sounded, I was about to write; but I heard a voice from the sky saying, “Seal up the things which the seven thunders said, and don’t write them.” The angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land lifted up his right hand to the sky, and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things that are in it, the earth and the things that are in it, and the sea and the things that are in it, that there will no longer be delay, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound, then the mystery of God is finished, as he declared to his servants, the prophets.

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.
echoes.note: The figure who raises his hand(s) to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever is the dominant template; Rev compresses Daniel's two hands to one but keeps the gesture, the oath formula, and the eschatological 'time' question. Very high verbal volume and recurrence.

echoes.text: For I lift up my hand to heaven and declare, as I live forever,
echoes.note: 'I lift up my hand to heaven and say, As I live forever' is the source oath formula behind 'lifted up his right hand... swore by him who lives forever.' Strong verbal correspondence (hand to heaven + living-forever oath).

echoes.text: But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run back and forth, and knowledge shall be increased.”
echoes.note: 'Seal up the words... shut up the book' directly underlies 'Seal up the things which the seven thunders said.' Inverts/echoes Daniel's sealing; Rev 22:10 later unseals. High thematic and verbal coherence.

echoes.text: He said, Go your way, Daniel; for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.
echoes.note: 'the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end' reinforces the sealing command of v.4 and the 'mystery finished' of v.7. Recurrence of Dan 12 cluster strengthens the reading.

echoes.text: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.
echoes.note: 'Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret (sod) to his servants the prophets' is echoed almost verbatim in 'the mystery of God... as he declared to his servants, the prophets.' Strong verbal volume.

echoes.text: One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?
echoes.note: The question 'how long until the end of these wonders?' is answered by the angel's oath 'there will no longer be delay,' tying Rev's oath to Daniel's interrogation of the man clothed in linen. Coheres with vv.4,7,9.

echoes.text: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: 'the vision... will not delay (lo yeacher)' / LXX 'it will not delay' underlies 'there will no longer be delay (chronos).' The LXX rendering with chronos/delay strengthens the verbal link; flagged LXX-vs-Hebrew (MT 'tarry', LXX delay) divergence.

echoes.text: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
echoes.note: 'you have made heaven... the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them' is the closest creation-formula parallel to the triadic 'heaven... earth... sea and the things in them' of the oath. Strong verbal volume for the creation clause.

echoes.text: for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
echoes.note: 'the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them' supplies the Decalogue creation triad sworn by; alternative or parallel source to Neh 9:6 for the same formula.

echoes.text: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;
echoes.note: 'who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps faith forever' couples the creation triad with the everlasting-living God, paralleling both halves of the oath.

echoes.text: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever; for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.
echoes.note: 'I blessed... him who lives forever' (Nebuchadnezzar's doxology) is a further attestation of the 'living forever' divine epithet sworn by here; faint, reinforces Dan 12:7 and Deut 32:40.

echoes.text: Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth,
echoes.note: Abram 'lifted up my hand to the LORD, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth' combines the raised-hand oath with the creator epithet, a faint patriarchal antecedent of the gesture-plus-creation oath.

pericopes.text: The voice which I heard from heaven, again speaking with me, said, “Go, take the book which is open in the hand of the angel who stands on the sea and on the land.” I went to the angel, telling him to give me the little book. He said to me, “Take it, and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.” I took the little book out of the angel’s hand, and ate it up. It was as sweet as honey in my mouth. When I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter. They told me, “You must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.”

echoes.text: But you, son of man, hear what I tell you; don’t be rebellious like that rebellious house: open your mouth, and eat that which I give you. When I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me; and, behold, a scroll of a book was therein; He spread it before me: and it was written within and without; and there were written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe. He said to me, Son of man, eat that which you find. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the […]
echoes.note: The prophet commanded to take and eat the scroll, which is 'in your mouth as sweet as honey,' is the controlling source for the whole eating-the-scroll scene. Highest verbal volume and recurrence in the chapter; Rev adds the bitterness in the stomach.

echoes.text: He said to me, Son of man, go to the house of Israel, and speak my words to them.
echoes.note: 'Go to the house of Israel and speak my words to them' commissions the prophet immediately after eating the scroll, paralleling 'You must prophesy again' in v.11. Continues the Ezek 2-3 commissioning sequence.

echoes.text: So the Spirit lifted me up, and took me away; and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; and the hand of Yahweh was strong on me.
echoes.note: 'I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit' after the scroll supplies the bitterness Rev locates in the stomach, a detail absent from Ezek 3:3 itself. Explains Rev's bitter/sweet contrast as a fusion of Ezek 3:3 and 3:14.

echoes.text: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
echoes.note: 'I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms' supplies the universal scope ('many peoples, nations... and kings') of the renewed prophetic commission in v.11. Coheres with Jeremiah's call narrative.

echoes.text: Your words were found, and I ate them; and your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart: for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies.
echoes.note: 'Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became... the joy of my heart' parallels ingesting the divine word as sweet; reinforces the Ezekiel scroll-eating with a Jeremianic eating-the-word motif.

echoes.text: How sweet are your promises to my taste, more than honey to my mouth!
echoes.note: 'How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth' supplies the sweetness-as-honey simile for the ingested word. Strong verbal echo on 'sweet as honey in my mouth.'

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'all peoples, nations, and languages' is Daniel's fourfold/threefold universal formula, recurring in Rev's 'many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.' Rev's list is a Danielic idiom though not from this verse alone.

echoes.text: You also, son of man, take a tile, and lay it before yourself, and portray on it a city, even Jerusalem:
echoes.note: The continuation of Ezekiel's sign-acts after the scroll (siege of Jerusalem) frames eating-the-scroll as prelude to enacted prophecy against peoples; faint structural echo supporting the 'prophesy again' commission.

echoes.text: More to be desired are they than gold, yes, than much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and the extract of the honeycomb.
echoes.note: God's ordinances are 'sweeter than honey and drippings of the honeycomb,' a second honey-sweetness-of-the-word parallel alongside Ps 119:103; faint, reinforces the simile.

pericopes.text: A reed like a rod was given to me. Someone said, “Rise, and measure God’s temple, and the altar, and those who worship in it. Leave out the court which is outside of the temple, and don’t measure it, for it has been given to the nations. They will tread the holy city under foot for forty-two months.

echoes.text: He brought me there; and, behold, there was a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass, with a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate. The man said to me, Son of man, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart on all that I shall show you; for, to the intent that I may show them to you, you are brought here: declare all that you see to the house of Israel. Behold, a wall on the outside […]
echoes.note: The measuring reed (kalamos / qaneh) given to a visionary to measure the temple is the controlling image; Ezekiel's bronze-bright man with a 'measuring reed' (40:3,5) measures the eschatological temple. Strong on volume (the rare measuring-reed motif), recurrence (Ezekiel's temple tour recurs across Rev's new-temple theology), and thematic coherence. LXX kalamos metrou matches Rev's kalamos.

echoes.text: I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, a man with a measuring line in his hand. Then I asked, “Where are you going?” He said to me, “To measure Jerusalem, to see what is its breadth and what is its length.”
echoes.note: The man with a measuring line sent 'to measure Jerusalem.' Reinforces the prophetic measuring-for-protection topos; in Zechariah measuring marks the city as guarded by God. High coherence with Rev's protective measuring of worshipers even as the outer court is surrendered. Hebrew chevel middah / LXX schoinion geometrikon (a line, not a reed) — note the instrument diverges (line vs. reed), so Ezekiel is the closer verbal parallel.

echoes.text: Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, How long shall be the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot?
echoes.note: The sanctuary and host 'trampled underfoot' (LXX katapateo) for a fixed number of days; Rev's 'tread the holy city under foot' echoes this Danielic profanation-of-the-holy-place with a numbered duration. Strong on the trampling verb and the apocalyptic time-limit structure.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: Forty-two months = 'time, times, and half a time' (3.5 years), the Danielic measure of the saints handed over to the oppressor. Recurs across Rev (11:2,3; 12:6,14; 13:5). Coherence with the broader Daniel-7 beast/persecution matrix is strong; the numerical symbolism is the load-bearing link.

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.
echoes.note: 'A time, times, and half a time' for the shattering of the holy people — the parallel Danielic statement of the 3.5-year limit underlying the forty-two months. Slightly fainter than 7:25 as the verbal source but thematically twinned.

echoes.text: Your holy people possessed it but a little while: our adversaries have trodden down your sanctuary.
echoes.note: Adversaries have 'trodden down' the sanctuary; supplies the OT lament-tradition of the holy place trampled by enemies that colors Rev's 'tread the holy city under foot.' Coherent but more diffuse than Dan 8:13.

echoes.text: God, the nations have come into your inheritance. They have defiled your holy temple. They have laid Jerusalem in heaps.
echoes.note: The nations have entered God's inheritance, defiled the holy temple, and reduced Jerusalem to rubble; grounds the 'given to the nations' / holy-city motif of Rev 11:2 in the temple-desecration lament. Provides the 'nations' (ethne) trampling Jerusalem complex.

echoes.text: He measured it on the four sides: it had a wall around it, the length five hundred, and the breadth five hundred, to make a separation between that which was holy and that which was common.
echoes.note: The measuring of the temple's surrounding wall to 'separate the holy from the common' — possible background for distinguishing the measured sanctuary from the unmeasured, surrendered outer court. Faint; conceptual only.

echoes.text: You shall measure outside of the city for the east side two thousand cubits, and for the south side two thousand cubits, and for the west side two thousand cubits, and for the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall be the suburbs of their cities.
echoes.note: Measuring/marking out sacred and civic space; very faint conceptual contribution to the measuring-for-allotment imagery. Included for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: I will give power to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy one thousand two hundred sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.” These are the two olive trees and the two lamp stands, standing before the Lord of the earth. If anyone desires to harm them, fire proceeds out of their mouth and devours their enemies. If anyone desires to harm them, he must be killed in this way. These have the power to shut up the sky, that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy. They have power over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague, as often as they desire.

echoes.text: Then I asked him, “What are these two olive trees on the right side of the lamp stand and on the left side of it?” I asked him the second time, “What are these two olive branches, which are beside the two golden spouts, that pour the golden oil out of themselves?” He answered me, “Don’t you know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.” Then he said, “These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.”
echoes.note: The two olive trees and (in Rev) two lampstands 'standing before the Lord of the whole earth' is a near-verbatim adoption of Zechariah's vision of the two anointed ones who stand before the Lord. Highest volume and distinctiveness in the pericope; Rev splits Zechariah's single lampstand into two but keeps 'standing before the Lord of the earth' as a fixed tag. LXX 'two sons of fatness' (oil) = the anointed pair.

echoes.text: He said to me, “What do you see?” I said, “I have seen, and behold, a lamp stand all of gold, with its bowl on the top of it, and its seven lamps on it; there are seven pipes to each of the lamps, which are on the top of it; and two olive trees by it, one on the right side of the bowl, and the other on the left side of it.”
echoes.note: The lampstand flanked by two olive trees supplying oil — the source image Rev compresses into 'two olive trees and two lampstands.' Together with 4:11–14 this is the structural backbone of the witnesses' identity.

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: Elijah's power to 'shut up the sky' so it does not rain — Rev's witnesses literally have 'power to shut up the sky, that it may not rain.' One witness is figured on Elijah. Strong verbal and thematic coherence; recurrence with the drought of 1 Kings 17–18 and Luke 4:25 / James 5:17 tradition.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “In this you shall know that I am Yahweh. Behold, I will strike with the rod that is in my hand on the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood. The fish that are in the river shall die, and the river shall become foul; and the Egyptians shall loathe to drink water from the river.”’” Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your rod, and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, over their […]
echoes.note: Moses turning the waters to blood (first plague) — Rev's witnesses have 'power over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague.' The other witness is figured on Moses. The plague-language ('strike... with every plague,' plege) is distinctively Exodus. LXX haima for the Nile-to-blood sign.

echoes.text: Elijah answered to the captain of fifty, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” Fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty.
echoes.note: Elijah calls down fire from heaven that consumes those sent to seize him; Rev's 'fire proceeds out of their mouth and devours their enemies' fuses this Elijah fire-judgment with the prophetic word. Strong on the fire-consumes-enemies motif and the Elijah figural pairing.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Armies, “Because you speak this word, behold, I will make my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them.
echoes.note: God makes his word in Jeremiah's mouth 'fire' that devours the people 'like wood' — supplies the specific image of fire issuing from the prophet's mouth (logos-as-fire), which 2 Kings alone does not (there fire falls from heaven). Best verbal explanation of 'fire proceeds out of their mouth.' LXX pyr in the prophet's mouth.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: 1,260 days = the 3.5-year Danielic measure (here as days rather than months, cf. 11:2). Ties the witnesses' prophetic period to the saints' appointed time of testimony/oppression. Recurrent across Rev's time-symbolism.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: The expected return of Elijah before the day of the Lord undergirds the eschatological-prophet typology applied to the witnesses; supports the Elijah identification beyond 1–2 Kings. Coherent with Rev's two-witness/Elijah figure.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: Valid testimony requires 'two witnesses'; the legal two-witness norm plausibly motivates Rev's pairing (martyres) and the courtroom 'testimony' language of 11:7. Conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Fire came out from Yahweh, and devoured the two hundred fifty men who offered the incense.
echoes.note: Fire from the LORD devours the rebels against Moses — a Mosaic counterpart to the Elijah fire-judgment, reinforcing 'fire... devours their enemies' from the Moses side of the pairing. Faint; secondary to Jer 5:14 and 2 Kings 1.

echoes.text: Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
echoes.note: Sackcloth as the garb of mourning/penitential prophecy (broadly OT, e.g. also Isa 22:12; Jonah 3:5). 'Clothed in sackcloth' draws on the general prophetic-mourning convention rather than one verse; cited as representative. Faint.

pericopes.text: When they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war with them, and overcome them, and kill them. Their dead bodies will be in the street of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified. From among the peoples, tribes, languages, and nations people will look at their dead bodies for three and a half days, and will not allow their dead bodies to be laid in a tomb. Those who dwell on the earth rejoice over them, and they will be glad. They will give gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the earth.

echoes.text: I saw, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them;
echoes.note: The horn/beast 'made war with the saints and prevailed against them' — Rev's 'the beast... will make war with them, and overcome them' is a near-quotation, including the verb 'make war' and 'overcome/prevail.' Strong volume and recurrence (cf. Rev 13:7). LXX/Theodotion epoiei polemon... katischysen.

echoes.text: Four great animals came up from the sea, diverse one from another.
echoes.note: The beasts 'come up' from the sea/deep; Rev's 'beast that comes up out of the abyss' fuses this Danielic ascent-of-the-beast with the Abyss motif. Supports the beast's provenance imagery.

echoes.text: They have given the dead bodies of your servants to be food for the birds of the sky, the flesh of your saints to the animals of the earth. Their blood they have shed like water around Jerusalem. There was no one to bury them.
echoes.note: The bodies of God's servants given as food, blood poured out 'and no one to bury them' — Rev's corpses left unburied 'in the street' and denied a tomb directly enacts this lament of the unburied dead. Strong thematic coherence with the desecration of the slain saints. LXX preserves the 'none to bury' motif.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.
echoes.note: Sodom as the type-city of wickedness destroyed by God; 'the great city... spiritually called Sodom' names the persecuting city by this archetype. Strong on the figural naming convention Rev signals with 'spiritually (pneumatikos).'

echoes.text: Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah. Hear Yahweh’s word, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah!
echoes.note: Isaiah addresses Jerusalem's rulers as 'rulers of Sodom' and people as 'people of Gomorrah' — the precedent for applying 'Sodom' figurally to the covenant city. Best explains Rev's pairing of Jerusalem-as-Sodom-and-Egypt and the spiritual renaming.

echoes.text: Your elder sister is Samaria, who dwells at your left hand, she and her daughters; and your younger sister, who dwells at your right hand, is Sodom and her daughters. Yet you have not walked in their ways, nor done after their abominations; but, soon you were more corrupt than they in all your ways. As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, Sodom your sister has not done, she nor her daughters, as you have done, you and your daughters. Behold, this was the […]
echoes.note: Jerusalem likened to her 'sister Sodom'; reinforces the prophetic tradition of naming the unfaithful holy city 'Sodom.' Coherent supporting witness to Isa 1.

echoes.text: The Egyptians ruthlessly made the children of Israel serve, and they made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and in brick, and in all kinds of service in the field, all their service, in which they ruthlessly made them serve.
echoes.note: 'Egypt' as the archetypal house of bondage and oppression of God's people; supplies the second half of 'Sodom and Egypt' as a figural name for the persecuting city. Thematic/typological rather than verbal.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: The 'three and a half days' the bodies lie exposed mirrors, in miniature, the 3.5 time-unit of Danielic affliction (years/months/days across the chapter). The half-week of death/dishonor compresses the persecution measure. Symbolic link.

echoes.text: Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the unwalled towns, make the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, a good day, and a day of sending presents of food to one another. Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, both near and far, to enjoin them that they should keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month Adar yearly, as the days in which […]
echoes.note: Enemies' defeat celebrated by 'sending gifts to one another' (Purim) — possible inversion behind 'they will give gifts to one another' as the earth-dwellers celebrate the prophets' death. Verbal contact ('gifts to one another') but ironic reversal; contested.

pericopes.text: After the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered into them, and they stood on their feet. Great fear fell on those who saw them. I heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” They went up into heaven in the cloud, and their enemies saw them. In that day there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified, and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe is past. Behold, the third woe comes quickly.

echoes.text: Thus says the Lord Yahweh to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live.
echoes.note: 'I will cause breath/spirit to enter you, and you shall live' — Rev's 'the breath of life from God entered into them' is a direct adoption of the dry-bones revivification oracle. Highest volume in the pericope. LXX pneuma zoes entering the slain matches Rev's pneuma zoes.

echoes.text: So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
echoes.note: 'The breath came into them, and they lived, and stood on their feet' — Rev's 'they stood on their feet' is virtually verbatim from this verse. Together with 37:5 the resurrection of the witnesses is a tableau of Ezekiel 37. LXX estesan epi ton podon auton.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Elijah taken up to heaven (in a whirlwind, with chariot of fire); Rev's witnesses 'went up into heaven in the cloud' completes the Elijah typology of the pair. Strong figural coherence; the cloud-ascent caps the Elijah identification (cf. also the Lord's ascension, Acts 1:9).

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: God breathing the 'breath of life' (pnoe/pneuma zoes) into the man — the creation source for the phrase 'breath of life,' which Ezek 37 itself reworks. Rev's wording sits atop this Genesis stratum.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: 'After the three and a half days' again invokes the Danielic 3.5 measure (here the death-interval reversed by resurrection). Maintains the chapter's pervasive half-week symbolism.

echoes.text: For in my jealousy and in the fire of my wrath have I spoken, Surely in that day there shall be a great shaking in the land of Israel; so that the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the animals of the field, and all creeping things who creep on the earth, and all the men who are on the surface of the earth, shall shake at my presence, and the mountains shall be thrown down, and the steep places shall fall, and every wall shall fall to the […]
echoes.note: The 'great earthquake' in the day of the LORD before which all tremble — supplies the eschatological earthquake-and-terror of Rev 11:13. Coherent with Rev's seismic theophany vocabulary (recurs at 6:12; 16:18).

echoes.text: Yet will I leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.”
echoes.note: The 'seven thousand' Elijah is told remain faithful — possibly inverted in Rev's 'seven thousand people were killed,' a deliberate reversal of the Elijah remnant number. Numerically distinctive enough to register; contested as intentional.

echoes.text: Joshua said to Achan, “My son, please give glory to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done! Don’t hide it from me!”
echoes.note: 'Give glory to the God of Israel/heaven' as the formula of compelled acknowledgment under judgment; background for 'the rest... gave glory to the God of heaven.' Faint, formulaic.

pericopes.text: The seventh angel sounded, and great voices in heaven followed, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” The twenty-four elders, who sit on their thrones before God’s throne, fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying: “We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, the one who is and who was; because you have taken your great power, and reigned. The nations were angry, and your wrath came, as did the time for the dead to be judged, and to give your bondservants the prophets, their reward, as well as to the saints, and those who fear your name, to the small and the great; and to destroy those who destroy the earth.” God’s temple that is in heaven was opened, and the ark of the Lord’s covenant was seen in his temple. Lightnings, sounds, thunders, an earthquake, and great hail followed.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: 'The kings of the earth... against the LORD and against his Anointed (Christos)' — Rev's 'the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ' answers and reverses Ps 2's rebellion: the kingdom now belongs to God and his Anointed. Strong on the Lord-and-his-Christ pairing. LXX tou christou autou.

echoes.text: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
echoes.note: 'Why do the nations rage (ethne)?' — Rev's 'the nations were angry (orgisthesan)' directly cites the raging-nations of Ps 2:1, framing the seventh-trumpet judgment as Ps 2 fulfilled. LXX ephryaxan ethne; Rev recasts the verb but the nations-rage motif is unmistakable.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The one like a son of man is given an everlasting 'kingdom... that shall not pass away'; Rev's 'the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord... He will reign forever and ever' realizes this Danielic everlasting dominion. Strong coherence with Rev's enthronement theology. LXX basileia aionios.

echoes.text: until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.
echoes.note: Judgment 'given to the saints' and the time comes for them to possess the kingdom — undergirds Rev's 'the time for the dead to be judged, and to give... the saints... their reward.' Tightly coherent with the Daniel-7 judgment-and-kingdom sequence.

echoes.text: Yahweh shall reign forever and ever.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD will reign forever and ever' — the Song of the Sea acclamation Rev quotes as 'He will reign forever and ever.' Near-verbatim. LXX basileuon ton aiona kai ep' aiona kai eti. Strong distinctiveness for the eternal-reign refrain.

echoes.text: He said: “Yahweh will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the pastures of the shepherds will mourn, and the top of Carmel will wither.”
echoes.note: Background for the divine 'voices from heaven' theophanic acclamation; faint, generic prophetic-voice topos. Included for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: Yahweh reigns! Let the peoples tremble. He sits enthroned among the cherubim. Let the earth be moved.
echoes.note: 'The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble' — enthronement-psalm pattern (the LORD reigns / nations tremble) matching Rev's 'you have taken your great power, and reigned' over against the angry nations. Coherent with the enthronement-acclamation genre.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: The divine name 'I AM' lies behind Rev's 'the one who is and who was' (ho on kai ho en); LXX ho on at Exod 3:14 is the verbal root of Rev's tripartite name (here truncated as the kingdom now is, dropping 'who is to come'). Thematic/onomastic.

echoes.text: He will bless those who fear Yahweh, both small and great.
echoes.note: The LORD blesses 'those who fear him, both small and great' — Rev's 'those who fear your name, to the small and the great' adopts this fixed pair. Distinctive 'small and great' fear-the-name formula. LXX tous mikrous meta ton megalon.

echoes.text: The priests brought in the ark of the covenant of Yahweh to its place, into the oracle of the house, to the most holy place, even under the wings of the cherubim.
echoes.note: The ark of the covenant placed in the inner sanctuary; Rev's 'the ark of the Lord's covenant was seen in his temple' draws on the temple/ark theology — the heavenly counterpart of Solomon's ark-in-the-holy-of-holies now disclosed. Coherent with Rev's heavenly-temple frame.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain. Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]
echoes.note: Sinai theophany — 'thunders, lightnings... and the whole mountain trembled' — supplies the 'lightnings, sounds, thunders, an earthquake' storm-theophany formula closing the chapter. Recurs as a Rev refrain (4:5; 8:5; 16:18); covenant-at-Sinai resonance fits the just-revealed ark of the covenant.

echoes.text: With pestilence and with blood will I enter into judgment with him; and I will rain on him, and on his hordes, and on the many peoples who are with him, an overflowing shower, and great hailstones, fire, and sulfur.
echoes.note: Judgment with 'great hailstones' in the day of the LORD — background for Rev's 'great hail' in the theophanic finale. Faint, one element of the storm formula.

pericopes.text: A great sign was seen in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was with child. She cried out in pain, laboring to give birth. Another sign was seen in heaven. Behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven crowns. His tail drew one third of the stars of the sky, and threw them to the earth. The dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she gave birth he might devour her child.

echoes.text: He dreamed yet another dream, and told it to his brothers, and said, “Behold, I have dreamed yet another dream: and behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me.”
echoes.note: Joseph's second dream — sun, moon, and eleven stars bowing — supplies the celestial trio (sun, moon, stars) clothing the woman. Strong volume and recurrence: the only OT passage joining all three luminaries with a person; the twelve stars cohere with the patriarchal/tribal symbolism (Joseph + eleven = twelve).

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.
echoes.note: Daughter Zion as a woman writhing and crying out in birth pangs (LXX ōdinousa kai krazei) closely matches 'cried out in pain, laboring to give birth' (krazei ōdinousa). Thematic + verbal correspondence for the laboring-woman = people of God figure.

echoes.text: After this I saw in the night visions, and, behold, a fourth animal, awesome and powerful, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet: and it was diverse from all the animals that were before it; and it had ten horns.
echoes.note: The fourth beast 'with ten horns' (Dan 7:7,24) feeds the dragon's ten horns; Daniel's composite-beast imagery underlies the seven-headed ten-horned monster (recombined in Rev 13). Recurrence of Danielic beast schema.

echoes.text: It grew great, even to the army of the sky; and some of the army and of the stars it cast down to the ground, and trampled on them.
echoes.note: The little horn that 'grew up to the host of heaven, and cast down some of the host and of the stars to the ground, and trampled on them' supplies the tail casting a third of the stars to earth. Verbal: stars cast down to the earth.

echoes.text: Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail; for now you will go out of the city, and will dwell in the field, and will come even to Babylon. There you will be rescued. There Yahweh will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.
echoes.note: 'Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail' — Zion in birth pangs fleeing to the wilderness/Babylon, then rescued. Reinforces the laboring-woman = Zion motif; anticipates 12:6 flight.

echoes.text: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son.
echoes.note: Zion gives birth before her pangs / brings forth a man child — birth imagery for the eschatological deliverance of God's people; pairs with the male child of 12:5.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: The protoevangelium enmity between the serpent and the woman and her seed underlies the dragon poised to devour the woman's child. Foundational figural frame for the whole chapter (cf. 12:9 'old serpent', 12:17 'rest of her offspring').

echoes.text: In that day, Yahweh with his hard and great and strong sword will punish leviathan, the fleeing serpent, and leviathan the twisted serpent; and he will kill the dragon that is in the sea.
echoes.note: Yahweh punishes Leviathan, the fleeing/twisting serpent, the dragon (LXX drakonta) that is in the sea — a chief OT source for 'great red dragon' (drakōn). Recurrence with 12:9; combat-myth backdrop.

echoes.text: You divided the sea by your strength. You broke the heads of the sea monsters in the waters.
echoes.note: 'You broke the heads of the sea monsters' / Leviathan (Ps 74:13–14) — multi-headed chaos dragon supplies the dragon's multiple heads; ancient Chaoskampf imagery. LXX kephalas tōn drakontōn.

echoes.text: Speak and say, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great monster that lies in the midst of his rivers, that has said, ‘My river is my own, and I have made it for myself.’
echoes.note: Pharaoh as 'the great dragon (LXX drakonta) that lies in the midst of his rivers' — imperial power figured as the river-dragon; contributes to dragon = oppressive empire and to the river/flood of 12:15.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of Yahweh; awake, as in the days of old, the generations of ancient times. Isn’t it you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the monster?
echoes.note: 'Are you not it that cut Rahab in pieces, that pierced the monster (LXX drakonta)?' — the primeval dragon-slaying recalled as paradigm for new exodus; faint reinforcement of the dragon motif.

echoes.text: Yes, it magnified itself, even to the prince of the army; and it took away from him the continual burnt offering, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down.
echoes.note: Continuation of the little-horn assault on the host/prince of the host; faint reinforcement of the star-casting and the dragon's standing-before-to-devour posture.

echoes.text: when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
echoes.note: 'When the morning stars sang together' — stars as heavenly host/angels frames the third of the stars as fallen angels (cf. 12:9). Faint, contested association of stars with angels.

pericopes.text: She gave birth to a son, a male child, who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron. Her child was caught up to God, and to his throne. The woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that there they may nourish her one thousand two hundred sixty days.

echoes.text: You shall break them with a rod of iron. You shall dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.”
echoes.note: 'You shall rule them with a rod of iron' — near-verbatim source for the male child who 'is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron' (poimanei en rhabdō sidēra). Rev follows LXX poimanei (shepherd/rule) over Hebrew tero'em (break). Repeated in Rev 2:27; 19:15.

echoes.text: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son.
echoes.note: 'Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a male child (LXX eteken arsen)' — the rare phrase 'male child' (arsen) is lexically distinctive and Zion brings forth a son. High volume and recurrence.

echoes.text: Who has heard such a thing? who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she gave birth to her children.
echoes.note: 'As soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children' — corporate birth of the nation; supports reading the woman as Zion/people of God who bears the child.

echoes.text: Therefore he will abandon them until the time that she who is in labor gives birth. Then the rest of his brothers will return to the children of Israel.
echoes.note: 'Until the time that she who is in labor has given birth' — the laboring woman whose offspring is the messianic ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd (5:4). Birth-of-the-ruler typology parallels the rod-of-iron shepherd.

echoes.text: Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well.
echoes.note: Moses (the deliverer-child threatened at birth) flees to the wilderness/Midian; broad exodus-flight typology behind the woman's flight to a prepared wilderness place. Faint.

echoes.text: “Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan.
echoes.note: Elijah hidden and fed (nourished) in the wilderness by God's provision (brook Cherith / ravens) — pattern of the faithful sustained in the wilderness during persecution. Faint analogy to being 'nourished' for 1260 days.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: 'A time, times, and half a time' — the 1260 days (3.5 years) reckons the same Danielic period of tribulation; numeric allusion rather than verbal. Explicit verbal echo surfaces at 12:14.

pericopes.text: There was war in the sky. Michael and his angels made war on the dragon. The dragon and his angels made war. They didn’t prevail, neither was a place found for him any more in heaven. The great dragon was thrown down, the old serpent, he who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him. I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation, the power, and the Kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ has come; for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night. They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death. Therefore rejoice, heavens, and you who dwell in them. Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil has gone down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has but a short time.”

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: 'At that time Michael shall stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people' — Michael as the angelic champion/prince in the eschatological crisis. Names Michael and his protective warfare for God's people.

echoes.text: But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days; but, behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me: and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
echoes.note: 'Michael, one of the chief princes' wars against the prince of Persia — establishes Michael as warrior-angel engaged in heavenly combat, the direct backdrop for 'Michael and his angels made war on the dragon.'

echoes.text: But I will tell you that which is inscribed in the writing of truth: and there is no one who holds with me against these, but Michael your prince.”
echoes.note: 'Michael your prince' — the only one who contends alongside the angelic messenger; reinforces Michael's role as captain of the heavenly host arrayed against hostile powers.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
echoes.note: 'the old serpent' (ho ophis ho archaios) identifies the dragon with the Eden serpent of Gen 3:1,14 — explicit retrospective naming binding the chapter to the protoevangelium. High lexical link (serpent).

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary.
echoes.note: Satan standing at the right hand to accuse (LXX antikeisthai) Joshua the high priest before the angel of Yahweh — paradigm for 'the accuser of our brothers... who accuses them before our God day and night.' Satan-as-prosecutor in the heavenly court.

echoes.text: Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Does Job fear God for nothing?
echoes.note: The Satan (ha-satan) in the heavenly council accusing Job (Job 1:9–11; 2:4–5) — the accuser figure 'day and night' before God; underlies 'the accuser of our brothers.'

echoes.text: How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low!
echoes.note: 'How you are fallen from heaven, Day Star (Lucifer), son of the morning! ...cast down to the earth' — the heaven-to-earth casting-down of a rebel celestial figure underlies the dragon being 'thrown down to the earth.' Often read with Luke 10:18.

echoes.text: By the abundance of your traffic they filled your midst with violence, and you have sinned: therefore I have cast you as profane out of the mountain of God; and I have destroyed you, covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.
echoes.note: The guardian cherub cast out / cast down from the mountain of God for pride and violence — secondary 'fall' tradition contributing to the heavenly expulsion of the adversary. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice. Let the sea roar, and its fullness!
echoes.note: 'Let the heavens be glad... let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar' — the call for heavens to rejoice (and earth/sea contrast) echoes the doxological summons 'rejoice, heavens... Woe to the earth and to the sea.' Faint formulaic parallel.

echoes.text: Sing, heavens; and be joyful, earth; and break out into singing, mountains: for Yahweh has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted.
echoes.note: 'Sing, heavens; and be joyful, earth' — prophetic summons to the cosmos to rejoice at God's salvation; faint parallel to the heavenly rejoicing of 12:12.

pericopes.text: When the dragon saw that he was thrown down to the earth, he persecuted the woman who gave birth to the male child. Two wings of the great eagle were given to the woman, that she might fly into the wilderness to her place, so that she might be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, from the face of the serpent. The serpent spewed water out of his mouth after the woman like a river, that he might cause her to be carried away by the stream. The earth helped the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed up the river which the dragon spewed out of his mouth. The dragon grew angry with the woman, and went away to make war with the rest of her seed, who keep God’s commandments and hold Jesus’ testimony.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: 'they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time' — near-verbatim source for 'a time, and times, and half a time' (kairon kai kairous kai hēmisu kairou); fixes the 3.5-year tribulation period of the woman's nourishment.

echoes.text: ‘You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings, and brought you to myself.
echoes.note: 'I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you to myself' — the eagle-wings given to the woman recall God carrying Israel out of Egypt into the wilderness. Strong exodus typology: deliverance into the wilderness.

echoes.text: As an eagle that stirs up her nest, that flutters over her young, he spread abroad his wings, he took them, he bore them on his feathers.
echoes.note: 'As an eagle... spreads abroad her wings, takes them, bears them on her pinions' (in the wilderness, 32:10) — eagle bearing Israel through the wilderness; pairs with Exod 19:4 as source of the great eagle's wings.

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.
echoes.note: 'a time, times, and a half' — the man clothed in linen swears the duration of the shattering of the holy people; reinforces and confirms the Danielic time-period applied to the woman's protection.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
